newsitem.title: USA: Ford sales dip 4.3 percent on slower truck sales.
newsitem.headline: Ford sales dip 4.3 percent on slower truck sales.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. reported Monday that its U.S. light vehicle sales fell 4.3 percent in April, a larger drop than analysts expected as light truck sales rose a scant half a percent because of shipping problems.

Ford's results pulled down the industry's total U.S. sales for April light vehicle to 1,279,751, a 3.8 percent decline from a year ago. The seasonally adjusted annual rate for April was 14.3 million units -- the lowest seasonal rate in 18 months. Consumers bought vehicles at a rate of 15.8 million units in March, and 15.1 million in April 1996.
Analysts said the slowdown was not unexpected after the strong 15.5 million light vehicle rate the industry averaged during the first quarter.
"At the moment, I think it looks more like a pause than a collapse," said Burnham Securities Inc. analyst David Healy.

Contributing to the industry decline were low supplies of Japanese vehicles after strong sales pushes in March, analysts said. The seasonal rate was hurt by unfavorable factors from the U.S. Commerce Department that are used to compute the seasonally adjusted selling rate, analysts said.

Ford, the nation's No. 2 automaker, sold 318,392 light vehicles in April, down from 332,777 a year ago. Car sales fell 10.7 percent to 130,175. Light trucks, the segment that includes pickup trucks, minivans and sport utilty vehicles, rose to 188,217 from 187,034.
Ford blamed the slight rise in its truck sales on a shortage of rail cars used to move new vehicles.

"Our dealers could have delivered even more trucks to their customers in April were it not for a shortage of bi-level rail cars to transport new trucks," said Bob Rewey, Ford's group vice president of marketing and sales.

Ford spokesman Joel Pitcoff said Ford lost no more than 5,000 vehicles because of the shipping problem. Worst hit was the Windstar minivan, although Explorer sport utility vehicles and F-Series pickup trucks were also hurt.
The problem is likely to continue through the second quarter, when truck output is at its peak levels, said Rewey. He said Ford is looking at "every possible alternative" to expedite shipments.
Analysts said the rail car issue may explain some of the sales declines, but not all of them, such as the 19.4 percent drop in Explorer sales.

Chris Cedergren, an automotive consultant with Nextrend Inc in Thousand Oaks, Calif., said the Explorer is being hurt by the enormously popular full-size Expedition. But he said the 14.6 percent fall in F-Series sales to 64,730 is another indication the once-hot light truck segment is beginning to cool.
"It's very subtle, but you could clearly make the statement the movement from luxury cars into trucks has slowed considerably," he said.

Along those lines, Cedergren noted the success of European brands, such as Mercedes-Benz, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG. Mercedes on Monday reported April U.S. sales of 9,315, its best April sales ever. Mercedes has sold 33,870 cars in the U.S. so far this year, also a record for a four-month sales period.

But Ford, which has some of the hottest selling pickup truck and sport utility vehicles on the market, said it increased its North American second quarter truck production forecast by 10,000 units to 750,000. That is an 11 percent increase over the 1996 second quarter.

Ford said it has received more than 9,000 dealer orders for its new Lincoln Navigator full-size sport utility vehicle. The Navigator, a luxury version of the Ford Expedition, is due to go on sale July 1.

On the car side, Taurus sales fell 7.2 percent to 29,758, and are off 3.9 percent to 117,893 for the first four months of 1997. That puts its well behind Toyota Motor Corp.'s Camry. Sales of the Camry sedan are up 28.6 percent to 138,721 so far this year.
General Motors Corp. last week reported a 5.4 percent drop in sales to 413,443. Chrysler Corp.'s sales tumbled 11.5 percent to 204,080.
